newsitem.title: UK: Gulf Canada lashes out at Clyde defence.
newsitem.headline: Gulf Canada lashes out at Clyde defence.

text.p: Gulf Canada Resources Ltd hit out at bid target Clyde Petroleum, saying the British company used the wrong method and the wrong numbers in its effort to defend itself against the 432 million stg offer.
"The logic they used is...inappropriate and the methodology is unprecedented," Dick Auchinleck, Gulf Canada's senior vice president of international and marketing, told Reuters.
He dismissed Clyde's defence document, released on Sunday, as "thin soup".
"There is no meat in this document at all," he said.
Auchinleck added Clyde should have looked at its net asset value rather than pointing at its cash flow multiple to defend itself against Gulf Canada's cash offer of 105 pence per share.
"NAV is used unfailingly by every single analyst certainly in this country and it is also the measure North American companies will use to value other companies," he said.
"The cash flow multiple itself is a very short term valuation measure," Auchinlek added.
He also claimed that in calculating the cash flow multiple, Clyde was using the closing share price on January 3, 1997 and the company's 1995 cash flow.
"That is really unprecendented. Cash flow analysis should really be about the future and not the past," Auchinleck said, adding that Clyde's cash flow was expected to fall in 1998 and 1999.
"You cannot really justify looking at the cash flow multiple for a business not showing a significant cash flow growth," he added.

The net asset value method is used by most British analysts and is based on a company's production from existing oil and gas reserves, ignoring exploration projects which might lead to new production in the future.

Given the long lifetime of oil and gas fields, the net asset value approach has a wider time horizon than the cash flow valuation, which is usually derived from expectations on a two to three year basis.
Analysts using the net asset value method praise its long- term view, allowing for a great variety of adjustable assumptions on such matters as tax and oil price.

Critics, however, claim too many assumptions have to be made to arrive at any firm conclusions. But some cash flow multiple supporters concede that the net value methodology can be useful for analysing small companies such as Clyde.
Richard Kent of Clyde's advisers Deutsche Morgan Grenfell said Clyde was inconsistent by making use of the cash flow valution this time.
He claimed the company justified its takeover of Australia's Crusader Ltd six months ago on the basis of the net asset value approach.
"It did not try to justify this by ratios of cash flow," Kent said.
Gulf Canada does not want to say what it believes is Clyde's net asset value. Auchinleck also declined to say what a fair cash flow multiple for Clyde would be.

In its defence document, Clyde said the bid put it on a cash flow multiple of 5.7 times, comparing unfavourably with comparable international companies trading on an historic multiple of 8.9 times and Gulf Canada on 12.7 times.
Analysts' estimates on Clyde's net asset value per share roughly range between 70 and 85 pence.
Clyde's shares firmed 1/2 a penny to 117 pence, but the premium over Gulf Canada's offer price did not worry the company or its advisers.
"It is normal at this stage to see the share price above the offer price," said Nigel Meek of Deutche Morgan Grenfell.
Clyde traded at 85 pence the day before Gulf Canada launched its hostile bid on December 18.
"The market prior to this offer reflected cash flow expectations for Clyde. I really don't think the increase is unusual," Auchinleck said.
-- Hans de Jongh, London Newsroom +44 171 542 7717
